Private Release  ·  October 1

THE IDENTITY TAX

How to Stop Paying for a Self You Never Chose

How much of your life are you sacrificing just to remain consistent with the person you think you are?

I'm not releasing this book the way books are normally released.

In fact, what I'm doing with it on October 1 is a little ridiculous.

But in order for you to understand why I'm doing it, I need to tell you how I got here.

Otherwise, none of this is going to make much sense.

So let me take you back to December 2023.

A Letter
From:
Benoit Malige
Tulum, Mexico
Tuesday morning.

Dear friend,

It's December 2023.

I'm standing in Fort Lauderdale Airport with one suitcase and a backpack. That's it. Everything I've decided I need for the next year is either on my back or sitting on the floor beside me.

I'm about to board a flight out of the United States, and for the first time in most of my adult life, I have no company to run, no employees waiting for me, no clients calling me, and no real answer to a question I used to answer without thinking:

Who the fuck am I now?

A few years earlier, that question would have been easy. I was the entrepreneur. I had built the successful company. Made the money. Bought the house. Bought the cars. Built the team. I had done most of the things I once believed would eventually make me feel like I had figured life out.

And the fucked-up part is that it worked.

I got the life I wanted. I just didn't want the life I got.

Worse, I had known that for quite some time. I felt the misalignment long before I did anything about it. But there was always another reason to keep going. People depended on me. The company was successful. Walking away from a life that was objectively working because it somehow felt wrong seemed insane.

So I stayed. Until eventually, I burned out badly enough that the decision was made for me. I shut down the company.

And when the thing I had spent years building disappeared, something else disappeared with it.

My identity.

Which is how I ended up standing in that airport with a suitcase, a backpack, and absolutely no fucking clue who I was without the life I had built around myself.

So I gave myself a year. To travel. To write. And, more than anything, to understand my own brain.

I wanted to know how a person could spend years building exactly the life he thought he wanted, realize it was making him miserable, know that, and still be unable to walk away.

I became obsessed with answering that question. And eventually, I got very, very good at it.

With no identity left to protect, I started questioning all of it. The things I believed. The things I wanted. The things I called personality. The things I thought were simply "me."

That work eventually became my newsletter, my videos, and then my first book, Unf*ck Your Thinking.

By the time I finished that book, I had accomplished almost exactly what the guy standing in Fort Lauderdale Airport had set out to accomplish.

I understood myself.

I got very good at seeing my patterns while I was repeating them. I could understand where a reaction came from, recognize what an old version of me was doing, and often know exactly what I should probably do instead.

There was just one problem.

Knowing why I was doing something did not mean I stopped doing it.

I had become extraordinarily self-aware. But awareness didn't give me agency.

I had learned how to watch myself live a life I already knew I didn't want.

And that left me with a more interesting question: If understanding yourself isn't enough to change your life, what is?

Benoit Malige
The Argument

You Don't Need Another Thing to Add to Your Life.

You've probably already tried adding more. Better habits. Better routines. More discipline. Therapy. Journaling. Books. Systems. More self-awareness.

Some of it probably helped.

But almost all of it starts with the same assumption: that the person you are right now is fundamentally the right person, and your job is to improve them.

The Identity Tax starts somewhere else.

The Old Way Add more.
  • Better habits
  • More discipline
  • More frameworks
  • More self-awareness
You get better at managing the person you already are.
The Identity Tax Subtract.
  • See what you've been carrying without realizing it.
  • Remove what you inherited, performed, or stopped questioning.
  • Choose what actually deserves to remain.
  • Build a life you authored, not performed.
You get your life back.

You Cannot Habit Your Way Out of Being Someone You Were Never Meant to Be.

You just get more disciplined at performing them.

The Point Isn't to Give You Better Answers.

It's to Give You Back the Authority to Answer for Yourself.

I don't want to replace one set of borrowed ideas with mine. The point is to help you see what has been deciding for you, remove what no longer deserves that authority, and put the pen back in your hand.

The book gives you authorship.

Les Essais

The Book Ends. The Practice Doesn't.

The Protocol ends too. I don't want the practice to.

The point of The Identity Tax isn't to replace your old answers with mine. It's to give you back the authority to form your own. The Protocol gives you a way to act on that. But authorship is something you practice.

And to be clear, this isn't a writing workshop. Writing is simply where we practice. The thing we're training is judgment.

I started writing because I had too many fucking thoughts and needed somewhere to put them. But a blank page kept doing something useful to me. It forced me to stop collecting other people's conclusions and produce one of my own.

You can read forever without deciding what you think. A blank page eventually stops letting you hide. You have to decide. What do I think? Why? What would change my mind?

Do that often enough and you start developing something considerably more useful than another collection of answers. Judgment. Taste.

Information isn't scarce anymore. Answers aren't scarce anymore. Increasingly, even intelligence isn't particularly scarce. What becomes scarce is knowing which answer matters. What to ignore. What deserves your attention.

Whatever you do, judgment sits on top of it. Better tools make you faster at your job. Judgment makes you better at deciding what the job requires in the first place.

In an economy where almost everyone has access to extraordinary amounts of information and intelligence, the ability to form your own judgment is becoming a luxury. A very valuable one to possess.

Michel de Montaigne called his attempts at thinking on paper Essais. In French, essayer means to try, to attempt, to test. I love that. So I'm stealing the idea and turning it into something we can practice together.

A monthly practice in judgment & taste

LES ESSAIS DE BENOÎT & ___

I Attempt

One question I genuinely don't know the answer to. I think it through on paper and mail you what I find.

You Attempt

You read it, challenge it, write against it, change your mind, and arrive at your own conclusion.

We Repeat

A new question every month. A continuing practice in judgment, taste, and independent thought.

And you're not going to have to imagine what this practice feels like. Your first issue is included in October.

Around the third week, I'll put it in an envelope and send it to your house. You'll read it. Think about it. Write against it. Come to your own conclusions. And we'll go through the first one together.

I'd rather put it in your hands.
